title: Peregrine Dataworks - Hybrid Connector exploratory
next_steps: Maya to send SOC2 + network diagram link
Diego to propose benchmark plan and GPU sizing spreadsheet
Customer to confirm compliance scope and target regions by 2029-04-08
Schedule follow-up technical deep-dive w/ kernel team (2 weeks)
action_items: Maya Chen: Share security pack (SOC2 summary, dataflow diagram, KMS notes) by 2029-04-03
Diego Alvarez: Draft suggested GPU pool sizes and batching config + spreadsheet by 2029-04-05
Samir Patel: Provide expected qps / latency SLOs and sample workload by 2029-04-06
summary: Intro/discovery with Peregrine Dataworks to scope hybrid GPU connector for sensitive workloads. Covered deployment modes (VPC vs on-prem connector), security requirements (KMS, audit logs, SSO), performance benchmarks, and potential pilot. Customer concerned about data residency, encryption, and model fallbacks. Agreed on follow-ups: send security artifacts, propose benchmark plan, schedule deeper technical session.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we're Maya and Diego from Redwood Inference. Uh, quick check on audio, can you all hear us?
[00:05] Samir Patel: Yep, loud and clear. Hi Maya, Diego, thanks for squeezing this in.
[00:10] Laura Ng: Hi, yes. Apologies for joining a minute late.
[00:12] Diego Alvarez: No worries. We're excited to dig in. Just to set expectations, this is a discovery to understand your infra, constraints, and what a pilot might look like.
[00:22] Samir Patel: Perfect. Quick context: Peregrine Dataworks runs real-time analytics products for financial customers, so PII and residency are... big deal. We're exploring hybrid onramp — some inference hosted, some on-prem.
[00:35] Maya Chen: Great, that matches a lot of customers we've done. Can you outline the high level: what's candidate workload, QPS, latency SLOs, and who the stakeholders are?
[00:44] Samir Patel: Sure. Primary workload is fraud-detection model scoring and a smaller chat assistant for ops. Expected peak qps ~350 req/s for scoring, 100 concurrent sessions for chat. Latency target is p95 < 120ms for scoring (very tight), chat can be 300-500ms. Stakeholders: me, Laura for infra, Vikram for SRE, legal/security will chime later.
[01:04] Laura Ng: And we have strict egress rules — customer data can't leave EU for some clients, so we need regional routing or on-prem for those tenants.
[01:13] Diego Alvarez: Understood. Two architectural patterns we typically propose: 1) Redwood Private (VPC connector) where control plane is separate but inference sits in your VPC; 2) On-prem box for fully air-gapped tenants. Both can share the same routing policy.
[01:28] Vikram Rao: Quick question — for VPC option, who manages keys? KMS in our cloud or Redwood? We need HSM-backed keys ideally.
[01:36] Maya Chen: Good point. We support customer-managed KMS (bring-your-own-KMS) and integrate with HSM-backed providers. Logs and audit trails remain accessible in your account, and we can produce audit log exports.
[01:50] Samir Patel: Okay. What about model fallbacks? If Dedicated capacity is saturated, do we have a graceful fallback to smaller quantized model? That's a hard requirement for availability.
[01:59] Diego Alvarez: Yep, we do smart routing and fallback policies. We can route by policy — latency-first routes to Dedicated GPU pools; cost or capacity fallbacks go to a quantized variant. There are gotchas with output parity; we'll want to test that on your eval prompts.
[02:15] Maya Chen: Also automatic prefix / KV cache can reduce token cost for scoring workloads. Though for scoring, often cache hit rate is low, but for chat assistant we see >40% prefix reuse in many setups.
[02:29] Samir Patel: Hmm, we need to be careful around cache TTL for sensitive data. If it's PII, we may not want to persist cache.
[02:36] Laura Ng: Exactly — caching is fine if tokenized data is hashed and then purged. Otherwise compliance won't let us.
[02:42] Diego Alvarez: We can make cache opt-in per route and set TTLs; also encrypted at rest with your KMS. I'll make a note to include cache policy examples.
[02:52] Maya Chen: Can you share a bit about your current infra — cloud provider, Kubernetes version, and whether you run custom inference stacks?
[02:59] Samir Patel: We run multi-region on AWS primarily (eu-west-1, eu-central-1), some GCP for internal tooling. K8s 1.25 in prod, using spot instances for batch. We don't have an existing LLM infra — currently use a third-party model host for a prototype.
[03:14] Maya Chen: Good baseline. For hybrid, we often recommend reserved capacity in Dedicated for steady traffic and VPC for data-surgical tenants. For EU-only tenants, a private sub-connector inside your eu-west-1 would work.
[03:27] Vikram Rao: About networking — what ports, and do we need an agent to run inside our VPC? How does control plane talk to data plane?
[03:36] Diego Alvarez: Our VPC connector is outbound-only; it opens an encrypted gRPC connection back to the control plane. No inbound exposure needed. Ports: standard egress 443 and optional high-throughput UDP for metrics; we provide a terraform module to install the connector.
[03:49] Laura Ng: Outbound-only is a big plus. Is the connector a container, VM, or appliance?
[03:54] Diego Alvarez: Typically a containerized service running as a DaemonSet, but we also provide an OVA for air-gapped envs.
[04:01] Samir Patel: Great. Security-wise, besides SOC 2 and KMS, what controls do you provide for role-based access, and can we integrate with our SSO (SAML)?
[04:11] Maya Chen: We support SAML/SO, OIDC, and RBAC policies at the token level. Token-level cost and latency breakdowns are in Redwood Console. For enterprise, we can enable session-based approvals and restrict model access by team.
[04:25] Samir Patel: What's the audit log retention? We need immutable logs for at least one year for some customers.
[04:31] Diego Alvarez: Retention is configurable — default 90 days, enterprise add-on can be 365 days with secure exports to your SIEM.
[04:39] Laura Ng: Cost is also a big gating factor — any idea on pricing for reserved Dedicated pools vs hosted per token?
[04:46] Maya Chen: We price hosted by tokens and embeddings, with clear unit economics. Dedicated is reserved monthly commit — we'd propose a sizing first and then provide a cost model. Diego will send a GPU sizing spreadsheet so you can model cost.
[04:58] Samir Patel: Nice. We have one more technical thing — KV cache consistency. For scoring we want deterministic outputs, so caching mustn't introduce nondeterminism.
[05:08] Diego Alvarez: The KV cache is TTL-based and deterministic — it caches transformer KV states for prefixes. However, there are edge cases with temperature and sampling; for scoring we recommend temperature=0 and use deterministic decode paths. We'll validate that in benchmarks.
[05:24] Samir Patel: Good. Also, quantization — we need to understand accuracy delta between fp16 and int8 quantized variants.
[05:32] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely. We run offline evals and also live canary tests; Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles based on workload. We'll include accuracy/regression numbers from our prior runs but we'll want to run them on your prompts.
[05:44] Maya Chen: Quick note — do you have any internal constraints on pilot timing? When could we realistically start a small pilot?
[05:50] Samir Patel: We want to be ramping in Q2, target pilot kickoff mid-May. Legal needs to confirm compliance scope but infra team can start technical verification earlier.
[05:59] Maya Chen: Sounds feasible. We'll aim to deliver the security pack this week and a benchmark plan next week. Diego, any notes on benchmarking approach?
[06:08] Diego Alvarez: For the benchmark, we propose three lanes: 1) steady-state scoring at target qps for p95 latency, 2) chat 95th percentile latency with concurrency, 3) failover/fallback tests with quantized model. We'll need sample prompts and representative payloads.
[06:25] Vikram Rao: We can provide a sample dataset and replay harness. Also want to run tests in eu-west-1.
[06:31] Diego Alvarez: Great. We'll include region-specific configs.
[06:36] Samir Patel: One worry — how do you handle secrets on the connector? Secrets for model files, KMS keys etc.
[06:43] Maya Chen: Secrets are stored in your cloud KMS. The connector reads ephemeral tokens and never persists plaintext keys. We can also integrate with HashiCorp Vault if you use it.
[06:54] Laura Ng: That would be preferred — we use Vault for secrets.
[06:58] Diego Alvarez: We support Vault integrations and can show a reference deployment.
[07:03] Samir Patel: Another question — if we do a hybrid split, do you support routing traffic by tenant ID, region, and cost tier?
[07:11] Maya Chen: Yes, policy-based routing supports tenant ID, region, and can include cost tags. You can pin tenants to private deployments.
[07:19] Samir Patel: Great. Can we talk about SLOs and how Redwood measures / enforces them?
[07:24] Diego Alvarez: We expose per-request latency traces and have per-route SLO monitoring. For Dedicated pools, we commit to throughput SLAs under the reserved capacity agreement. If SLOs slip, automatic fallback to alternate pools or quantized variants is configured.
[07:38] Laura Ng: Will we get alerting integrations? PagerDuty, Slack?
[07:42] Maya Chen: Yep, Redwood Console supports webhook and PagerDuty integrations.
[07:46] Samir Patel: Perfect. Any notable limitations we should know about?
[07:51] Diego Alvarez: A couple: 1) Quantized models can diverge slightly — we'll measure regression on your evals; 2) Cold-starts for very long contexts can add latency — our continuous batching reduces this but real numbers will come from bench.
[08:05] Maya Chen: Also, for air-gapped setups, iteration cycles are slower for model upgrades — we'd need a slightly different ops process.
[08:13] Samir Patel: Makes sense. We're okay with managed upgrades as long as we control the approval.
[08:18] Diego Alvarez: We'll support canary rollouts and require customers to approve major model changes for private instances.
[08:26] Samir Patel: Could you point us to any reference architecture docs or case studies for regulated customers?
[08:31] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll share the security pack with a reference architecture PDF and a case study of a fintech customer that used VPC connector + Dedicated pools.
[08:41] Vikram Rao: When you say Dedicated pools, are those multi-tenant across customers? We need absolute isolation for some regulated clients.
[08:49] Diego Alvarez: Dedicated pools are single-tenant to the commit — compute is isolated to your account. We can also allocate particular GPUs for absolute physical isolation.
[08:59] Laura Ng: That would be useful to note in the pricing sheet.
[09:03] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll include both shared dedicated (logical isolation) and physically isolated GPU pricing.
[09:10] Samir Patel: For the pilot, what minimum commit would you recommend?
[09:14] Diego Alvarez: For a small pilot, we often recommend a modest Dedicated slice that covers peak qps for one tenant plus VPC connector for EU-only tenants. We'll propose numbers in the sizing sheet.
[09:25] Maya Chen: Ok. Shifting gears, any competitor concerns we should know? Are you evaluating any other vendors?
[09:30] Samir Patel: Yes, we're comparing CloudGiantAI and FlowServe for pricing. CloudGiantAI has better token pricing but opaque performance numbers; FlowServe offers on-prem appliances.
[09:40] Maya Chen: We can share transparent benchmark reports and are open to running side-by-side tests.
[09:45] Vikram Rao: Side-by-side would be ideal. We'll also want to test edge cases with large context windows.
[09:52] Diego Alvarez: Totally — we'll design the bench harness to exercise large contexts and memory usage, and measure kv cache effectiveness.
[09:59] Samir Patel: One last operational ask: can we get an SLA for model rollout windows so we can coordinate change freezes with clients?
[10:06] Maya Chen: Yes, for enterprise customers we can negotiate maintenance windows and require approvals.
[10:11] Laura Ng: That aligns with our change management.
[10:15] Samir Patel: Ok, looks like we're aligned. Next steps?
[10:19] Maya Chen: Recap: Maya will send security pack (SOC2 summary, network diagram, KMS notes) and reference architecture; Diego will share GPU sizing and benchmark plan/spreadsheet; Peregrine to provide sample workloads and confirm pilot timing. We'll schedule a technical deep-dive in two weeks.
[10:35] Vikram Rao: We'll aim to get the sample harness and SLOs to you by next Friday.
[10:39] Maya Chen: Awesome. Anything else?
[10:42] Samir Patel: No, that's good. Thanks.
[10:44] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites and links.
[10:49] Diego Alvarez: Thanks all.
[10:52] Laura Ng: Bye.

Notes: transcription shows occasional mis-heard words (KV cash vs KV cache), speaker overlap at 00:10. Shared artifacts referenced: security-pack.pdf (link), gpu-sizing-template.xlsx (link), benchmark-plan.md (link).

End of transcript.
